rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Tables 2, 5-7 report the authors' own long-term field experiment (2010-19, data analysed for 2018-19) in a Sicilian orange orchard, with stem water potential, sap flow, soil water content, yield, fruit quality and WUE measured under four irrigation treatments (FI, SDI, RDI, PRD) in a randomised block design.
rows.notes: The study is a primary field trial of deficit irrigation strategies (sustained DI, regulated DI, partial root-zone drying) applied through surface/sub-surface drip in an orange orchard, with irrigation scheduled by the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith approach and adjusted with soil-moisture probe readings. It does not test or evaluate app-based or 'smart' irrigation scheduling, so it provides no evidence of its own on the technology named in the claim row (app_scheduling). What it actually shows: DI treatments saved 17-53% of irrigation water (Table 2) over a decade without significant reductions in yield (Table 5) or fruit quality (TA, TSS, MI; Table 6), while PRD gave WUE values about 2-3 times those of full irrigation (Table 7); <U+03A8>stem in PRD reached -1.8 to -2.0 MPa and SF-VPD/SF-Tair slopes were lower under DI (Figs. 2-6). The authors interpret this as long-term adaptation of the trees to water deficit, which is relevant to water-saving deficit irrigation under water scarcity, but not to app-based scheduling as a climate-risk-management technology. Single site, single cultivar, plot scale; results reported with standard errors for yield, quality and WUE, but these do not bear on the claimed technology.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study concerns deficit irrigation regimes (SDI, RDI, PRD) in citrus; the review cites it under 'water-saving technologies, smart irrigation' but the claim row's coded technology (app_scheduling) does not match anything the study tests.
